draft.bar: Exploratory draft. Not an announcement. Internal brainstorm for a potential 2027 campaign.

footer.tag: Exploratory campaign for 22nd Ward Alderperson. Little Village / La Villita, Chicago.
footer.note: This is an internal brainstorm to visualize what a campaign could look like. Nothing here is a declaration of candidacy. All figures and dates should be verified before any public use. Latina Sweat Project is a 501(c)(3) and is not affiliated with any campaign.

home.lede: Vanessa Tirado is a Little Village social worker who helped build a community wellness institution from nothing. She is exploring a run for 22nd Ward alderperson because La Villita deserves a choice, not a handoff.
home.built_h: We didn't wait for a title. We built it.
home.built_lede: In 2022 a handful of Latinas started pop-up yoga in Little Village parks and mutual aid inside migrant shelters. Vanessa helped turn that into the Latina Sweat Project: daily programming on the Southwest Side, thousands of free classes, nearly a hundred neighbors trained as teachers on full scholarships, meals and coats and school supplies for families when they needed them.
home.b3: free community events she helped lead
home.built_foot: Figures are the Latina Sweat Project's public reporting, shown as biography. LSP is a 501(c)(3) and does not endorse candidates. Verify before public use.
home.meet_h: Raised on these blocks. Still here.
home.meet_p1: Vanessa Tirado grew up in Little Village and lives here today. She earned her Master of Social Work at UIC and has spent more than ten years as a licensed school social worker, sitting with Chicago kids and families through the hardest moments of their lives.
home.meet_p2: She is a co-founder and director of the Latina Sweat Project, chairs its Culture and Ethics board, and teaches the classes herself. She knows what it costs to build something in this neighborhood, and what it feels like when a landlord decides it's over.
home.plan_lede: La Villita stood up to the raids. Now it has to be rebuilt by someone who has actually built something here. Seven planks, each with a mechanism a 22nd Ward alderperson actually controls.
home.plank_cta_p: The recovery compact signed, the tax help desk open, free fitness in three parks, participatory budgeting launched.
home.choice_h: This seat has been passed down for forty years. We're asking for it the other way: from you.
home.choice_p: García to Muñoz to Rodriguez, and now the incumbent's chief of staff, announced the day after he stepped aside. Nobody is questioning anyone's courage or commitment to this community. We are questioning the process. A seat can be handed down. A vote can't.
home.d1_p: 5 p.m. at the Board of Elections. 473 valid signatures required; we file three times that.
home.d2_p: After the objection fights are over, the names are final.
home.d3_p: Mail ballots go out the same day. Vota temprano.
home.d4_p: If nobody clears 50% on February 23, the top two meet again on April 6.
home.close_q: "Health is not a luxury. It is a neighborhood."
home.close_cite: Draft closing line, for Vanessa to make her own
home.p1_p: A recovery compact in the first 100 days: rent-bridge micro-grants through the SSA, a vacant-to-vibrant storefront program, and a vendor licensing fix that finally lets elotes be made on the cart.
home.p2_p: Free weekly fitness in every ward park with local instructors, a yearly Ward Health Report Card, diabetes prevention where people already go, and clean air treated as a health policy.
home.p3_p: Defense is the floor. Add family preparedness clinics, trauma care for kids in ward schools, and quarterly public briefings with both police districts on any contact with federal agents.
home.p4_p: A property-tax help desk with mobile clinics on the Cicero corridor, a campaign against predatory home buyers, and a public, community-driven zoning process.
home.p5_p: Protect the violence-intervention gains, light the blocks with repeated incidents, expand Safe Passage, and guarantee summer jobs for ward teens.
home.p6_p: Every kid plays: free leagues in ward parks, a paid youth council with its own budget, and a fight for mental-health staff at Farragut and the Little Village Lawndale campus.
home.p7_es: Tu voz, tu voto, tu presupuesto
home.p7_p: Participatory budgeting on the $1.5M menu, every zoning decision online with the reason, and a pledge never to hand-pick a successor or double as committeeperson.

join.lede: A campaign is not a website. It is Saturday mornings on 26th Street, a notarized petition sheet, and a February morning at the polls. Here is where you fit in.
join.now_h: The petition sprint: 473 required, 1,500 is the goal.
join.p1_p: Official forms only. Registered voters who live in the 22nd Ward. Print clearly, one signature per line, and you sign the circulator statement in front of a notary.
join.p2_p: Filing opens 9 a.m. Monday Oct 19 in the Pedway outside the Board of Elections. Everyone in line at opening enters the lottery for the top ballot line. Deadline: 5 p.m. Monday Oct 26.
join.p3_p: Expect objections from the ward organization. Over-file, have every sheet reviewed by a lawyer before filing, and keep circulators reachable for hearings. Certification is Dec 17.
join.form_h: Tell us your block and what you're good at.
join.form_lede: One hour or one hundred, there's a spot for you. This prototype form does not submit anywhere yet. In production it posts to a Google Form through a hidden iframe, the same pattern used on byronfor25.com.
join.step1: A real person texts you within 48 hours.
join.step2: You pick a standing date: Saturday walk or Wednesday open table.
join.step3: You bring one neighbor the first time. Then another.
join.f_petition: Bring the petition to me so I can sign it
join.f_done: Prototype only: nothing was sent. In the live site this is where the "what happens next" message appears.
join.f_sms: By signing up you agree to receive texts from the campaign. Reply STOP to opt out.
join.fund_h: Can't walk with us today? Chip in.
join.fund_p: A $27 average donation from neighbors is how a challenger stays unbought. Donation links go live once a committee is registered with the Illinois State Board of Elections.
join.r1_p: Oct 5 to Oct 24. Carry an official sheet, collect signatures from registered 22nd Ward voters, get it notarized. The single most important job right now.
join.r2_p: Ten neighbors, your kitchen table, forty-five minutes with Vanessa. We bring the pan dulce.
join.r3_p: Saturday mornings, start on 26th Street. Knock doors with a partner, end with a group stretch.
join.r4_p: Spanish-speaking callers and canvassers for the half of the ward that votes in Spanish.
join.r5_p: Notarize circulator statements; help review sheets before Oct 26 and defend them in objection hearings.
join.r6_p: Voter-file lookups, signature validation, graphics for the group chat, video for Instagram.

meet.h1: A Little Village daughter who never left.
meet.lede: Born and raised in La Villita, and still living here. A licensed school social worker with more than a decade of work with Chicago youth and families, and a builder who helped turn pop-up yoga classes in Little Village into a citywide wellness movement.
meet.story_h: Social worker first. Organizer by necessity.
meet.story_p1: Vanessa grew up in Little Village and earned her Master of Social Work at the University of Illinois Chicago. For more than ten years she has worked as a licensed school social worker, sitting across the table from kids and parents in crisis, navigating CPS, hospitals, and the systems that too often fail families on the Southwest Side.
meet.story_p2: In 2022 she and a small group of Latinas started pop-up yoga classes in Little Village parks and mutual aid sessions inside migrant shelters. No grant, no building, no permission. That became the Latina Sweat Project: a nonprofit that has delivered thousands of free and discounted classes, trained nearly one hundred neighbors as certified teachers on full scholarships, and put food, clothing, and school supplies in the hands of families across the Southwest Side.
meet.story_p3: She has chaired the organization's Culture and Ethics board, co-chaired its annual gala, and spent her weekends on the floor of a studio with a hundred neighbors on mats. She knows what it takes to build something in this community, and what it feels like when a landlord decides it's over: in fall 2026 the organization was displaced from its first studio and is rebuilding.
meet.receipts_h: What she has already built with neighbors
meet.receipts_lede: Figures below are from the Latina Sweat Project's own public reporting and are shown as the organization's work. Each one is marked for verification before public use.
meet.s1: free community events she helped lead
meet.s2: free or discounted classes funded by community campaigns
meet.s3: neighbors certified as yoga teachers, tuition-free
meet.s4: in mutual aid and nonprofit support
meet.s6: back-to-school items for local kids in 2025
meet.s8: Black and Brown instructors hired or amplified
meet.receipts_foot: Source: latinasweatproject.com impact and about pages, Oct 2026. Verify each figure with LSP before it appears in any public material. LSP is a 501(c)(3) and does not endorse candidates.
meet.why_h: The ward office should work like the best community organizations already do.
meet.why_p1: Every week a social worker in Little Village watches a kid lose a semester to an asthma attack, a mother skip a doctor's visit because of fear on the street, a family of six squeezed into a two-flat they can no longer afford. The answers are not mysterious. They are organized. They just are not happening at the scale a ward office could make them happen.
meet.why_p2: Vanessa's case is simple: she has spent her career inside the systems that touch families here, and she has already built an institution from nothing with neighbors. The ward deserves someone who has done both.
meet.f1_p: Proud Mexican-American, raised in Little Village, lives in Little Village. Registered yoga instructor (Yoga Sculpt, Power Yoga).
meet.f2_p: Master of Social Work, University of Illinois Chicago. Licensed school social worker, trauma-informed care, 10+ years citywide.
meet.f3_p: Co-founder and director, Latina Sweat Project. Chair, Culture and Ethics board. Gala co-chair. Featured voice, 2026 gala at the MCA.

plan.h1: Small ward. Short clock. Clear math.
plan.lede: The 22nd Ward cast fewer than 5,000 votes for alderperson in 2023, across just 19 precincts. That is the whole game: about 2,000 votes to make the runoff on February 23, about 3,500 to win it on April 6.
plan.warn_p: Three weeks to collect about 2,200 raw signatures, with the ward organization's volunteers already circulating for its candidate and the Nov 3 general election soaking up every organizer in the city. The petition sprint is the campaign's first and hardest test.
plan.m2: Identified supporters (65% turn out with chase)
plan.h1b: Spanish at the door by default. Bilingual literature on every piece.
plan.h2: Walk voter-file lists only. Roughly a fifth to a third of residents are not citizens, and many households have no eligible voter.
plan.h3: Non-citizen neighbors can volunteer in every role except circulating petitions, donating, and voting. Never ask anyone about status.
plan.h4: Register 18-year-olds at the Little Village Lawndale campus and Farragut, and newly naturalized citizens. Same-day registration exists.
plan.h5: Permanent vote-by-mail enrollment for seniors from November so they get both the February and April ballots automatically.
plan.h6: Early voting at Toman Library, 2708 S. Pulaski (confirm for 2027). "Vota temprano" walks from house meetings.
plan.money_h: A cheap ward in dollars, an expensive one in hours.
plan.b1: by Oct 26: fifty founding donors and one launch house party
plan.b2: by Dec 31: call time, house parties, the year-end push that the press reads on Jan 15
plan.b3: by Feb 23, plus $125–175K more for a runoff
plan.l7: Literature, signs, voter file, events, compliance
plan.money_foot: Illinois limits for 2025–26: $7,300 per individual, $14,600 per union or corporation, $72,800 per PAC. Limits lift for everyone if any candidate self-funds, or an outside group spends, over $100,000. No cash over $250. City contractors and lobbyists capped at $1,500. Foreign nationals may not contribute. Verify all of this with counsel.
plan.end_h: Who is locked, who is open.
plan.e_locked_p: SEIU locals and state council, AFSCME 31, Chicago Federation of Labor, Teamsters 700, Chuy García's organization, the Latino Caucus, United Working Families (leans), Mujeres Latinas en Acción (the organization candidate sits on its board).
plan.e_open_p: Chicago Teachers Union, if Vanessa is a CPS clinician and member: member-to-member first. UNITE HERE Local 1. Teamsters locals with members along the Pulaski corridor. Illinois Nurses Association, Mijente, Better Streets, Urban Environmentalists via questionnaires.
plan.e_people_p: Ald. Julia Ramirez (12th): ask for advice before an endorsement; she is the model for this race. Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez (25th): keep warm privately, decide on a public tie only for the runoff. Kristian Armendariz: no attacks, a back channel for a mutual runoff endorsement.
plan.end_foot: Enlace, LVEJO, New Life Centers, Instituto del Progreso Latino, and The Resurrection Project are 501(c)(3)s and cannot endorse. Attend their forums; recruit their leaders only in a personal capacity.
plan.g1: Confirm the title. LSP's site lists Vanessa as "Director" in one place and "Co-Founder & Director" in another. Use one board-approved title everywhere.
plan.g2: Confirm her address is inside the post-2022 22nd Ward boundary and has been since at least Feb 23, 2026. Eastern Little Village sits in the 25th, 24th, and 12th.
plan.g3: Run the city debt check (water, tickets, fines) before filing. It is the most common way candidates get removed.
plan.g4: Confirm her employer. If CPS, follow the ethics policy strictly and lean into CTU membership.
plan.g5: Latina Sweat Project is a 501(c)(3). Vanessa takes a documented leave from its board. No LSP space, lists, staff time, accounts, or logos for the campaign. Bio references only.
plan.g6: Every number on this site must be verified and attributed before public use. Pick one defined figure per claim.
plan.g7: Audit personal social media back to 2015 before launch.
plan.g8: Write a one-line position on the issues an opponent will raise, including immigration enforcement and LSP's past solidarity actions, before launch.
plan.t1_n: Lawyer on retainer. Residency and city-debt check. Statement of Economic Interests filed. 25+ circulators, 3 notaries, nightly notary nights. Target 170 raw signatures a day.
plan.t2_n: If 1,600+ validated signatures are in hand by Oct 18, be in line at 9 a.m. Oct 19 for the top-ballot-line lottery.
plan.t3_n: 203 S. State St. Bound, numbered sheets. Statement of Candidacy, SEI receipt, full photocopy. Deadline 5 p.m. Oct 26.
plan.t4_n: Saturday event in the ward, Spanish first. Exclusive to Block Club the night before, then La Raza, Univision, Telemundo.
plan.t5_n: Expect a challenge from the ward organization. Records exam volunteers, rehab affidavits, legal reserve of $7.5K–$25K.
plan.t6_n: Three house meetings a week. Voter-ID canvass in the strongest precincts. Call time 10 hrs/week. Endorsement questionnaires.
plan.t7_n: Year-end push: the Q4 report due Jan 15 is how the press reads viability.
plan.t8_w: Mail ballots out, early voting opens
plan.t8_n: VBM chase begins. Mail piece 1 (bio). Candidate forums. Spanish radio starts Jan 18.
plan.t9_n: Four-day GOTV. Every identified supporter contacted three times. 19 precinct captains and poll watchers.
plan.t10_n: Goal: hold the organization candidate under 50% and finish second with about 2,000 votes.
plan.t11_n: Contact eliminated campaigns within 48 hours. Re-canvass their voters. Goal: 3,500 votes on April 6.

plat.lede: La Villita stood up to the raids. Now it needs to be rebuilt by someone who has actually built something here. Every plank below names the mechanism a 22nd Ward alderperson actually controls: the $1.5 million menu, the SSA, zoning, ordinances, CDPH, the Park District, the police district councils.
plat.100_h: What May 17 to August 25, 2027 looks like.
plat.h1b: Sign the 26th Street Recovery Compact with SSA #25 and the Chamber; launch the rent-bridge micro-grants.
plat.h2: Open the property-tax and anti-predatory-buyer help desk, with Cicero corridor clinics.
plat.h3: Start Parques Activos in at least three ward parks.
plat.h4: Launch participatory budgeting for the next menu cycle.
plat.h5: Hold the first ward safety table with both police districts and CVI partners.
plat.h6: Co-sponsor the Cumulative Impacts and street-vendor licensing ordinances.
plat.h7: Publish the baseline Ward Health Report Card.
plat.l1: Warm, active, true to who she is. Yard signs and ward walks.
plat.l2: Process contrast for mail, debates, and the runoff.
plat.l3: "Made here" pride. Echoes the Immigrant Made shirt in her headshot.
plat.lines_foot: Language guidance: say builder, rebuild, recovery, health is infrastructure, open ward office, block by block. Never say machine, corrupt, or puppet. Never comment on any opponent's age, gender, or detention. Never promise what sits in another ward: the Discount Mall, La Villita Park, and the county jail are not in the 22nd.
plat.p1_why: 26th Street does roughly $900 million a year in sales. During the 2025 federal immigration operation, businesses reported sales down 40 to 70 percent, and the Chamber heard from more than fifteen owners behind on rent in a single week. The city's response was a holiday trolley and social media spotlights.
plat.p1_c: Vanessa has run a small operation through a crisis. The organization she helps lead lost its studio to a building sale and kept its programming alive through pop-ups. She knows what rent, payroll, and a landlord's decision feel like.
plat.p1_i1: A 26th Street Recovery Compact in the first 100 days: SSA #25 commissioners, the Chamber, property owners, and street vendors at one table, with part of the SSA budget redirected to rent-bridge micro-grants, corridor security, and cleaning.
plat.p1_i2: A ward-office application desk, in Spanish, so every eligible storefront applies to Neighborhood Opportunity Fund and Community Development Grant rounds.
plat.p1_i3: Vacant to Vibrant: menu and SSA money for façades and lighting, and six-to-twelve-month pop-up-to-lease deals pairing empty storefronts with vendors, makers, and nonprofits.
plat.p1_i4: Co-sponsor a street-vendor licensing ordinance that legalizes safe on-cart preparation of elotes and fruta under CDPH standards, with shared commissary access.
plat.p1_i5: A year-round "Mercado de la 26" destination campaign with the Chamber and Choose Chicago, anchored on quinceañera season.
plat.p2_why: Most adults in South Lawndale are obese, and about one in two children. Nearly half of households in the surveyed Latino West Side areas are food-insecure. Every Save-A-Lot in Chicago has closed. Diesel traffic from the Hilco warehouse site runs past homes and schools. No candidate owns this issue, and it is Vanessa's life's work.
plat.p2_c: The ward's health record is COVID-era convening and reacting to Hilco after the fact. There is no standing plan for chronic disease, food, or fitness. "I've spent years getting our neighbors moving, stretching, and healing. I'll bring that to every park in the ward."
plat.p2_i1: A Ward Health Report Card every year with CDPH: diabetes, obesity, asthma, food access, and mental-health indicators by neighborhood, with public targets and an annual bilingual town hall.
plat.p2_i2: Parques Activos: free weekly bilingual fitness in every ward park through the Park District, taught by paid local certified instructors. Walking clubs, strength, family fitness, senior chair classes.
plat.p2_i3: Finish the Piotrowski Park natatorium with guaranteed free family swim and learn-to-swim hours for ward residents.
plat.p2_i4: Bring a Spanish-language, CDC-recognized diabetes prevention program to parks, schools, and parishes with local federally qualified health centers.
plat.p2_i5: Food access: recruit fruterías and bodegas into the city's $10,000 Neighborhood Market grants, and start a Piotrowski farmers market that takes LINK with a match.
plat.p2_i6: Clean air as health policy: co-sponsor the Hazel Johnson Cumulative Impacts Ordinance, enforce the Target-site truck route on Pulaski, and put community air monitors near schools.
plat.p2_i7: Push to extend the city's CARE alternate-response mental-health teams to the 10th and 8th districts, and bring a CDPH no-cost mental-health access point to the Southwest Side.
plat.p3_why: The 2025 operation brought 3,841 arrests citywide, with peak days in Little Village. Consulate registrations of U.S.-born children more than doubled as families planned for the next wave. Defense is the floor; everyone in this race stands on it. The next fight is preparation and recovery.
plat.p3_c: Not a contrast of courage. A contrast of scope. "Defending families is the floor. We agree on that. I'll also make sure families are prepared, kids are cared for, and the businesses that employ them survive."
plat.p3_i1: Support a ward legal fund and monthly in-ward legal clinics through the city's Legal Protection Fund and the Office of New Americans.
plat.p3_i2: Family Preparedness Plans: free clinics on short-term guardianship and power of attorney so no child is left without a caregiver after a detention, reaching parents through the school social-work networks Vanessa knows.
plat.p3_i3: Trauma care for kids: press CPS for added social workers and counselors at Farragut, the Little Village Lawndale campus, and the feeder elementaries. Trauma-informed summer programming in the parks.
plat.p3_i4: Hold CPD to the Welcoming City ordinance: a quarterly public briefing with the 10th and 8th District commanders and district councils on any contact with federal agents.
plat.p3_i5: Business continuity for immigrant-owned shops: bilingual "what to do if" guides and emergency staffing networks.
plat.p4_h: Stay in La Villita: homes and property taxes
plat.p4_why: The 2024 reassessment drove a record 16.7 percent jump in the median Chicago homeowner's bill, and about 30 percent on average across fifteen South and West Side neighborhoods. Investors send frightened families up to thirty solicitations a day, including fake "check" mailers. Half of renters are cost-burdened.
plat.p4_c: The ward committee took roughly $49,500 from the Assessor's campaign and from the Assessor personally in 2026, after the reassessment that drove the tax spike. Whose side was the ward office on when the bills came?
plat.p4_i1: A property-tax help desk at the ward office with monthly bilingual clinics alongside the Assessor and the Board of Review: exemptions, senior freeze, appeals, payment plans. Mobile clinics on the Cicero corridor.
plat.p4_i2: "No vendas con miedo": a campaign against predatory home buyers, referrals of deceptive mailers to the Attorney General, free housing counseling before any sale, and a disclosure ordinance for unsolicited purchase offers.
plat.p4_i3: Preserve two-flats and greystones: home-repair and ADU programs, a Little Village housing preservation ordinance modeled on Woodlawn's, and support for the neighborhood limited-equity co-op.
plat.p4_i4: A public, community-driven zoning process: every request published online, a community meeting before any aldermanic support for a major development, and a resident zoning advisory council with renters, owners, and business seats.
plat.p4_i5: No property-tax increase on homeowners. Protect small businesses. Targeted revenue from the largest entities only if it is legally durable.
plat.p5_why: 2025 had the fewest homicides citywide since 1965, and Little Village was a focus area with real drops. Shootings continue on 26th Street and the side streets, and federal money for community violence intervention is being cut. Safer isn't safe yet.
plat.p5_c: The organization will claim the decline. Vanessa credits the people who did the work and focuses on what is next.
plat.p5_i1: Fight for continued community violence intervention funding in the city budget, and credit the outreach workers and residents who earned the decline.
plat.p5_i2: A monthly ward safety table with both police districts, CVI outreach workers, schools, and block clubs, with a one-page public data brief after each one.
plat.p5_i3: Menu money for street and alley lighting on blocks with repeated incidents, and expanded Safe Passage around Farragut and the Little Village Lawndale campus.
plat.p5_i4: A ward target for One Summer Chicago placements and year-round paid youth work as violence prevention.
plat.p5_i5: Coordinated patrols, lighting, and safety alerts with the Street Vendors Association on the routes vendors take home.
plat.p6_why: Farragut enrolls about 400 students. Little Village elementary schools lost almost a fifth of their students during the pandemic. Youth mental health is strained after the raids. Vanessa's professional credential is school social work.
plat.p6_c: Youth is shared ground with other challengers and a bridge for a runoff. The contrast with the organization is on delivery.
plat.p6_i1: Every Kid Plays: free youth sports, fitness, and girls' wellness leagues in ward parks, with menu money to repair fields and lighting.
plat.p6_i2: Defend neighborhood high schools: oppose cuts to the Little Village Lawndale campus and Farragut, push community-school status and mental-health staffing in the CPS budget.
plat.p6_i3: A paid Ward Youth Council with its own participatory-budgeting allocation.
plat.p6_i4: After 3 p.m. and summer: parks, libraries, and nonprofits paired for free programming, with no programs run by any organization tied to the alderperson's family or staff.
plat.p7_why: The seat passed from García in 1986 to Muñoz to Rodriguez, and now to the incumbent's chief of staff. In November 2025 the U.S. House formally rebuked the same succession pattern at the congressional level. This is not about any person. It is about how a neighborhood chooses.
plat.p7_c: "This seat has been handed down for forty years. I'm asking for it the other way, from you."
plat.p7_i1: Bring back participatory budgeting: residents vote every year on how to spend a share of the $1.5 million aldermanic menu. The 22nd was one of Chicago's first PB wards in 2013.
plat.p7_i2: Put it all online: menu spending by project and block, every zoning decision with the reason, every ward staff opening posted publicly.
plat.p7_i3: No dual role, no handoffs: a pledge not to serve as Democratic committeeperson while alderperson, and never to hand-pick a successor or time a departure to favor one.
plat.p7_i4: A ward office that comes to you: weekly Spanish-first ward nights and mobile office hours on the Cicero corridor, two miles from the office on 26th.
plat.p7_i5: An independent vote. "My vote belongs to La Villita, not to a mayor." A written explanation for every major budget vote.

race.h1: A narrow path. A real one.
race.lede: Internal analysis of the 2027 22nd Ward race from precinct-level Board of Elections results, campaign finance filings, and press coverage. Every projection is an estimate and is labeled as one.
race.k3: organization share in 2023, with challengers who had almost no money
race.k4: rough odds of forcing a runoff, with $150–250K raised
race.c1_p: Chief of staff to Ald. Rodriguez since 2023, elected 10th District police councilor in 2023 with about half of ward voters marking her name. Announced Sept 10, the day after the incumbent stepped aside, with Chuy García, Commissioner Alma Anaya, and Rodriguez behind her. Detained for seven hours by Border Patrol in Oct 2025 while documenting a raid. Would be the ward's first woman alderperson. Inherits a network whose committee held $222,211 in June 2026.
race.c1_f: Strengths: courage story, name recognition, labor and García network. Opening: the handoff itself, a staffer's record on 26th Street and taxes, never on the ballot in precincts 16–19.
race.c2_p: Youth and community organizer, Little Village Community Council circle. Took 18% in 2023 with about $1,700 on hand, strongest in north and central Little Village. Running again.
race.c2_f: A rival in February and an asset: his 15–18% is what keeps the organization under 50%. A runoff ally if he is treated with respect now.
race.c3_p: Little Village social worker, co-founder and director of a community wellness nonprofit. No ballot history, no committee yet, and a distinct lane nobody else owns: health, small-business recovery, and an open ward office.
race.c3_f: Base to build: Cicero corridor homeowners, 26th Street business owners, women 25–50 and parents who skipped 2023.
race.map_lede: In 2023 the anti-organization vote split in two: a youth and organizer vote in north-central Little Village, and a pragmatic homeowner vote on the Cicero corridor that went two-to-one for Vallas in the mayoral runoff. The corridor has the highest turnout in the ward and the weakest loyalty to the organization. That is where a builder's message lands first.
race.t_total: Total target to force a runoff (5,400-vote case)
race.pct_foot: Source: Chicago Board of Election Commissioners, Feb 28, 2023 municipal election. Precinct boundaries unchanged for 2027.
race.pa1: Raise $150,000 to $250,000. Nobody has ever tested this ward with a funded, credible challenger. Both prior challengers had under $2,000.
race.pa2: Armendariz stays in and holds 15 to 18 percent. Do not fight him for precincts 6 through 9. Concentrate on zones F, E, B, and 26th Street business owners.
race.pa3: Grow the electorate by 400 to 600 voters who are registered but skipped 2023: women, parents, fitness and school networks Vanessa reaches personally. Each new voter is worth about two points off the organization's share.
race.runoff_p: Win number: about 2,300 to 2,800. Vanessa's February 1,830 at 90% retention is about 1,650. Armendariz's 920 at 65% transfer with his endorsement is about 600. The last 450 to 550 come from Cicero-corridor homeowners who sat out February and from voters whose mayoral candidate lost. Pre-negotiate the runoff endorsement now, privately.
race.i1_p: The 2025 federal operation defines the race. The organization owns the defense story; the opening is the second year of the crisis: 26th Street sales down 40–70%, families preparing to leave.
race.i2_p: Record reassessment hikes hurt most on the homeowner precincts. The ward committee took about $49,500 from the Assessor's campaign and from him personally in 2026.
race.i3_p: Johnson sits near 23% approval and the incumbent is one of his closest allies. Independence from every mayoral camp is an asset. The ward voted no on Bring Chicago Home.
race.i4_p: Majority adult obesity, half of children, half of households food-insecure, every Save-A-Lot closed. Nobody owns this issue.
race.i5_p: The Discount Mall, La Villita Park, the county jail, and the 10th District station are in the 25th and 24th wards, not the 22nd. The ward spans the 10th and 8th police districts.
race.le1_p: Beat an appointed incumbent next door with SEIU money, a community-driven zoning pledge, and organizing through Instituto and Latinos Progresando. The closest model for this race. Ask for advice before an endorsement.
race.le2_p: Won an open seat on tenant and anti-displacement organizing and a no-developer-money pledge. Shares the 26th Street corridor, Crawford, vendors, and health clinics with the 22nd. Polarizing; decide on a public tie only for the runoff.
race.le3_p: "Machine" messaging alone got 9–14% in 2019 and 16–18% in 2023, with no money. The contrast must be builder versus successor, on substance, funded, with a lane nobody else owns.
race.foot: Full memo with sources: docs/research/01-race-dynamics.md in the project repository. Unverified items include the incumbent's December 2025 budget vote, whether participatory budgeting continued after 2015, and the exact ward edges near Cicero and Cermak.

race.zC: Little Village core and the 26th Street corridor
